_meta.purpose: STOF Injection Variants Knowledge Base -- OWASP WSTG/CWE-grounded reference patterns for stof/modules/injection_variants_tests.py (TC-134).
sources: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide -- WSTG-INPV-04 'Testing for HTTP Parameter Pollution'
PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- HTTP Parameter Pollution research (secondary support)
OWASP CSV Injection Cheat Sheet / CWE-1236 'Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File'
HackerOne #807961 (8x8) -- Blind OS command injection in a text-to-speech API, confirmed via response-time delay
HackerOne bug bounty guides (YesWeHack, HackerOne blog 'How To: Command Injections') -- sleep-based blind detection as the standard technique when command output isn't returned

HackerOne #2573567 (U.S. DoD), #500515 (Starbucks), #312543 (Semrush), #248668 (X/xAI SXMP processor) -- disclosed XXE reports, external entity file disclosure and SSRF via XML parsing (SOAP/sitemap/SXMP endpoints)
PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- XXE injection tutorial: classic external entity, blind XXE via out-of-band interaction, error-based XXE via a redefined parameter entity
HackerOne #1104349 (Glovo) -- Server-Side Template Injection via a user-controlled form field
HackTricks / AppSec Brief SSTI guides -- the {{7*7}}/${7*7}/<%= 7*7 %> arithmetic-evaluation polyglot as the standard, engine-agnostic detection oracle
HackerOne #1130721, #1130874, #1757676, #1458020 (Rocket.Chat) -- pre-auth and post-auth blind NoSQL injection via MongoDB $regex/$ne operators, escalating to account takeover and RCE
_meta.key_finding: Six distinct injection-variant shapes bundled into this one module (matching this project's own 'coherent test-case family, not one module per technique' convention): (1) HTTP Parameter Pollution and (2) CSV/Formula Injection (both pre-existing, see their own entries below), plus four newly added ones grounded in real disclosed reports: (3) OS Command Injection, detected the same time-based-blind way disclosed reports document (a sleep delay, since command output is rarely reflected); (4) XXE, detected via a differential external-entity file-read against a low-sensitivity canary file, with a parser-error fingerprint as a lower-confidence fallback (both real, disclosed-report-documented detection paths, distinct from PortSwigger's third path -- out-of-band collaborator confirmation -- which this project's existing SSRF TC-137.6 already establishes as a separate, not-yet-confirming technique); (5) SSTI, detected via the same engine-agnostic arithmetic-polyglot oracle real bug bounty guides converge on, which -- like xss_tests.py's DOM-XSS marker check -- proves evaluation occurred, not mere reflection; (6) NoSQL Injection, detected via the exact MongoDB operator-substitution pattern (`$ne`/`$gt` replacing a string password value) that repeatedly appears across real disclosed Rocket.Chat reports, reusing sqli_tests.py's own login-bypass success oracle (looks_json_authenticated) unchanged. All four new techniques stay within this project's 'candidate-detect, never auto-exploit' line: command injection never reads command output, XXE only ever targets a single low-sensitivity file, SSTI proves evaluation without attempting real code execution, and NoSQL injection confirms an auth bypass without extracting any real stored data.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Submit the SAME parameter name twice in one request (query string or form body) with two distinct benign values, after first taking a single-value baseline for EACH value separately. Compare the polluted response against both baselines.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered GET or POST endpoint carrying at least one known parameter (query string or form body) -- the duplicate is injected into whichever location the parameter already lives in.
patterns.real_example: WSTG-INPV-04's own documented pattern: a front-end WAF/validation layer inspects only the FIRST occurrence of a duplicated parameter while the back-end application framework uses the LAST (or vice versa), letting an attacker craft a request that passes the WAF's check on one value while the application acts on a different, unvalidated one.
patterns.evidence_signal: The polluted response either reflects BOTH submitted values together (proof some layer processed the duplicate unexpectedly), or matches NEITHER the first-value-only baseline NOR the last-value-only baseline (SequenceMatcher similarity below 0.95 against both) -- a response that simply matches one of the two expected baselines is the normal, unremarkable outcome and is never flagged.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as injection_variants_tests.py's _technique_hpp: two single-value baselines (send_probe, existing _injection_shared.py helper) taken first, then a duplicate-key request built directly via urlencode over an explicit list of (name, value) pairs (_send_duplicated_param) since a dict-based params mapping cannot express a repeated key. Gated behind allow_state_changing_probes since the POST variant resubmits a discovered form -- write-adjacent by this project's own conservative-by-default convention, even though the GET variant alone is read-only.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Plant a harmless, formula-shaped marker payload (a value beginning with =, +, -, or @, e.g. '=1+1+"<unique marker>"') into a discovered free-text POST field via a low-privilege authenticated context, then check via a SEPARATE, higher-privileged GET context whether the stored value is later returned verbatim -- no leading apostrophe/quote-escape, no stripped leading character.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Two-act, same shape as xss_tests.py's TC-128.4 and sqli_tests.py's TC-127.6: Endpoint A stores the value (a comment/feedback/profile free-text field); Endpoint B (a listing/detail/admin-review page) later renders it back, which is also the shape a CSV/Excel export of that same stored data would draw from.
patterns.real_example: OWASP's own CSV Injection Cheat Sheet PoC shape (=1+1, =cmd|'/c calc'!A1) and the broader CWE-1236 class: any application that lets a user-controlled field reach a CSV/Excel export unescaped is vulnerable to a formula executing in the recipient's spreadsheet application when they open it.
patterns.evidence_signal: The planted marker appears as a byte-for-byte substring of the verify-phase response with its leading =/+/-/@ character intact and NOT immediately preceded by a single-quote/apostrophe character in the response body -- the standard mitigation (force-text prefix) that would otherwise make the raw substring match a false positive.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as injection_variants_tests.py's _technique_csv_formula_injection, reusing _second_order_plant_candidates/_second_order_verify_candidates from _injection_shared.py unchanged (same free-text field heuristics as TC-127.6/TC-128.4). Framed honestly in the Finding description as a precondition only: STOF has no way to confirm a spreadsheet export of the stored data actually exists, so a hit means 'this value would survive into a CSV/Excel export unescaped IF one exists', never a confirmed CSV injection. Gated behind allow_state_changing_probes since the plant phase is a real POST.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Inject a bounded shell sleep payload (';sleep 6;', '|sleep 6', '$(sleep 6)', '`sleep 6`') into a discovered parameter and measure response latency against a baseline, requiring the delay to repeat once before reporting -- the exact same 'bounded, repeatable-before-reporting' discipline sqli_tests.py's TC-127.3 already established, applied to shell metacharacters instead of a SQL sleep function.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered GET or POST endpoint carrying at least one known parameter -- real disclosed reports (HackerOne #807961) show command injection landing in parameters that reach a shell/exec call server-side (a file-processing, conversion, or system-utility-wrapping endpoint), indistinguishable from any other parameter by name alone.
patterns.real_example: HackerOne #807961 (8x8): a text-to-speech API's input parameter reached a shell command unsanitized; the disclosed exploitation path used sleep-based timing since command output was never reflected in the response -- the standard technique cited across HackerOne's own 'How To: Command Injections' guide and multiple bug bounty writeups for exactly this blind case.
patterns.evidence_signal: A repeatable (confirmed twice) response-latency delta at or above the injected sleep duration, compared against an unmodified baseline request -- never a bare 'the response changed' or a single unconfirmed timing sample.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as injection_variants_tests.py's _technique_command_injection. Tries a short, bounded list of 4 separator styles per candidate endpoint (POSIX chaining, pipe, and both command-substitution forms), stopping at the first repeatable hit -- never summing multiple sleeps at once, the same DoS-risk restraint TC-127.3's own docstring establishes for a real, shared target this project doesn't own. Not gated behind allow_state_changing_probes (a single timing probe isn't gate-worthy, matching every other reflected-style injection technique in this codebase).

patterns.generalized_transformation: Re-submit a discovered POST endpoint with Content-Type: application/xml and a DOCTYPE declaring an external SYSTEM entity pointing at a low-sensitivity local file, compared against a structurally identical request with no DOCTYPE/entity at all -- a differential check, not a bare substring search, so an endpoint that just echoes its request body verbatim can never masquerade as a real external-entity read.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered POST endpoint, re-submitted with an XML body regardless of its normal Content-Type -- real disclosed XXE reports (Semrush #312543, X/xAI #248668) hit endpoints whose PRIMARY function has nothing to do with XML on the surface (a sitemap-audit feature, an SMS-processing servlet) but whose backend still auto-detects and parses an XML body.
patterns.real_example: PortSwigger's canonical classic-XXE payload: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]><foo>&xxe;</foo> -- STOF's version substitutes /etc/hostname (a single, low-sensitivity line) for /etc/passwd, matching this project's 'signal only, never claim to read real sensitive data' restraint. Real disclosed reports (DoD #2573567, Starbucks #500515) confirm the same external-entity-declaration shape against production XML-consuming endpoints.
patterns.evidence_signal: PRIMARY: the response contains real substituted content at the entity-reference position that a no-entity baseline request does not (proof of external file read). FALLBACK (lower confidence): a real XML/entity-parser error signature (SAXParseException, 'external entity', 'DOCTYPE is not allowed', ...) present in the payload response but absent from the baseline -- PortSwigger's own documented 'error-based XXE' path for when out-of-band/direct read is blocked.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as injection_variants_tests.py's _technique_xxe. Deliberately does NOT implement PortSwigger's third documented path (out-of-band interaction via a collaborator server) -- this project's existing SSRF TC-137.6 already sends a real OOB probe via burp.collaborator_url but explicitly does not poll for a received callback (see ssrf_tests.py's own docstring); a true blind-XXE-with-confirmed-callback technique is a separate, not-yet-built gap, not silently folded into this one.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Inject a polyglot arithmetic-expression payload combining multiple template engines' own syntax ({{a*b}} Jinja2/Twig, ${a*b} Freemarker/Thymeleaf/EL, <%= a*b %> ERB) with this run's own random operands, and check whether the computed PRODUCT appears in the response while the raw, un-evaluated payload text does not -- proof of server-side evaluation, never a claim that arbitrary code execution was achieved.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered GET or POST endpoint carrying at least one known parameter -- the disclosed Glovo report (#1104349) landed in an ordinary user-facing form field, no different in shape from any other injectable parameter.
patterns.real_example: The canonical, engine-agnostic SSTI detection payload documented across HackTricks, AppSec Brief, and multiple bug bounty guides: ${7*7}/{{7*7}} returning 49 in the response (rather than the literal, un-evaluated text) is the standard, tool-independent (tplmap and manual testing both use it) proof that user input reached a template engine's expression evaluator.
patterns.evidence_signal: The literal decimal product of this run's own two random operands appears in the response body, AND the raw payload string itself does not -- both conditions required, so a template engine that merely reflects the payload text verbatim (never evaluating it) can never read as a hit.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as injection_variants_tests.py's _technique_ssti. Random per-run operands (not a fixed 7*7) mean the expected product can never coincidentally already appear in a page's normal content. Not gated behind allow_state_changing_probes, same reasoning as TC-134.3 -- a single read-oriented probe isn't gate-worthy.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Substitute a JSON login request's password field (a plain string in a legitimate request) with a MongoDB query operator object ({"$ne": null} or {"$gt": ""}) instead -- the exact same shape sqli_tests.py's TC-127.4 uses for SQL login-bypass, just with an operator OBJECT where a string belongs rather than a crafted string value, since NoSQL query languages accept structured operators directly as field values.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: The same discovered POST endpoint find_login_endpoint (stof/modules/base.py) already locates for TC-127.4 -- a username-shaped and password-shaped parameter pair -- reused unchanged for this technique's JSON-body variant.
patterns.real_example: HackerOne #1130721 (Rocket.Chat): the getPasswordPolicy method's token parameter accepted a raw {"$regex": "^A"} object, enabling character-by-character blind extraction; #1130874 (also Rocket.Chat) found the same operator-injection shape reachable via the users.list API, both escalating to account takeover and eventually RCE once an admin account was compromised.
patterns.evidence_signal: An actually-authenticated-looking response (an auth-token-shaped JSON field present where a definitely-wrong-credentials baseline has none, or HTTP status below 400) when the operator payload is submitted -- never a bare non-error status code, since a rejected login can still return 200 with an error body.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as injection_variants_tests.py's _technique_nosql_injection. Reuses looks_json_authenticated (_injection_shared.py, already built for TC-127.4/auth_tests.py) unchanged for the success oracle -- the same JSON-API-shaped-success detection this project already validated works against real modern SPA backends (confirmed live against Juice Shop earlier in this project's history).
